title: Non-text Content
why: Screen reader users hear the alternative text instead of seeing the image. Without it they hear nothing, or a file name like "IMG_4032.jpg", and miss what the image communicates. The same applies to icons, charts and image buttons.
howToFix: For images from the media library, open the media item in Umbraco and fill in its alternative text field, or the alt text field on the block or picker where the image is used. Describe what the image tells the reader in this context, not what it looks like. For icons and image buttons in templates, developers add an accessible name (alt, aria-label or visually hidden text) that says what the control does.
caveats: Purely decorative images must have an empty alt (alt=""), not a description, or screen readers read out noise. Don't start with "Image of…" — screen readers already say it's an image. An image containing text needs that text in its alt. Charts and infographics need the information in the text or a nearby description, not just a short alt.
howToTest: Turn off images in the browser (or use a screen reader) and read the page: is anything missing that a sighted reader would get from the pictures? Check that decorative images are silent and that every meaningful image has alt text that makes sense in its sentence or section.

title: Audio-only and Video-only (Prerecorded)
why: People who are deaf can't hear an audio-only recording such as a podcast, and people who are blind can't see a video without sound. They need the same information in another form.
howToFix: Publish a text transcript next to audio-only content. For video without sound, add a text description or an audio track that describes what happens. A link to the transcript directly beside the player is enough.
caveats: Auto-generated transcripts need proofreading; names, numbers and technical terms are often wrong. A transcript that only exists in a PDF must itself be accessible.
howToTest: Find every audio-only and silent video on the site. For each, check there is a transcript or description nearby that contains everything the recording communicates.

title: Captions (Prerecorded)
why: Deaf and hard-of-hearing visitors, and anyone watching with the sound off, rely on captions to follow speech and important sounds in videos.
howToFix: Upload a caption file (WebVTT) with each video, or turn on and correct captions on YouTube/Vimeo before embedding. Captions must include who is speaking when that isn't obvious, and meaningful sounds such as [applause] or [alarm].
caveats: Automatic captions are a starting point, not a fix: they must be corrected. Captions burned into the image can't be resized or turned off, but they do count. Subtitles that only translate speech don't cover sound effects.
howToTest: Play each video with captions on. Check that captions exist, match what is said, are in sync, and include important non-speech sounds.

title: Audio Description or Media Alternative (Prerecorded)
why: Blind visitors miss information that is only shown visually in a video, such as on-screen text, charts or actions without narration.
howToFix: Either provide an audio description (a narrated version that describes the important visuals) or a full text alternative that describes both the speech and the visuals. For talking-head videos where everything is said aloud, no extra description is needed.
caveats: A transcript of the speech alone is not enough if important things happen on screen without being said. On-screen text such as names and titles counts as visual information.
howToTest: Listen to each video without watching. Is anything important missed, such as text on screen, a demonstration or a chart? If so, check for an audio description or a full text alternative.

title: Captions (Live)
why: Deaf and hard-of-hearing visitors can't follow live streams such as webinars or broadcast events without real-time captions.
howToFix: Use a streaming platform that supports live captions, ideally by a human captioner (CART) or a reviewed live captioning service, and turn them on for every live stream published on the site.
caveats: Machine live captions are often inaccurate for names and jargon. Once the stream becomes a recording, it also needs corrected captions under 1.2.2.
howToTest: Check the site for live streams. For each, confirm captions were available during the live broadcast.

title: Audio Description (Prerecorded)
why: Blind visitors need to know what happens visually in a video when it isn't explained by the soundtrack.
howToFix: Provide an audio-described version of the video, or record the video so that the narration describes everything important on screen. Plan this in the script; it's much cheaper than adding description afterwards.
caveats: At AA a text alternative alone is not enough; an audio description is required. Videos with only background music and visuals almost always need description.
howToTest: Listen to each video without watching. If visual information is missed, check that an audio-described version exists and is easy to find.

title: Sign Language (Prerecorded)
why: For many Deaf people sign language is their first language, and they understand it more easily than written captions.
howToFix: Provide a sign language interpretation for prerecorded videos, either embedded in the video or as a separate version.
caveats: This is a AAA criterion and costly; prioritise important videos such as service information. Use the sign language of your audience (e.g. Swedish Sign Language for a Swedish audience).
howToTest: Check that each prerecorded video with speech has a sign language version.

title: Extended Audio Description (Prerecorded)
why: Some videos pause too little for a normal audio description to fit, so blind users still miss information.
howToFix: Provide an extended audio description, where the video pauses so the description can play in full.
caveats: AAA. Only needed when normal audio description can't fit into the existing pauses.
howToTest: For videos with audio description, check that no important visual information is skipped because there was no time to describe it.

title: Media Alternative (Prerecorded)
why: A full text alternative lets deafblind users, and anyone who prefers reading, get all of a video's content through a braille display or text.
howToFix: Publish a full text version of each prerecorded video that includes the dialogue and descriptions of all important visual information.
caveats: AAA. A caption file alone is not a media alternative; it lacks the visual descriptions.
howToTest: For each prerecorded video, check that a full text alternative exists and contains both speech and visual information.

title: Audio-only (Live)
why: Deaf users can't follow live audio-only broadcasts, such as live radio or audio streams.
howToFix: Provide a live text alternative, such as real-time captions or a live transcript, for live audio-only content.
caveats: AAA. Rarely needed on typical websites.
howToTest: Check the site for live audio-only content and confirm a live text alternative is provided.

title: Info and Relationships
why: Screen readers rely on the page's structure — headings, lists, tables and form labels — to let users navigate and understand content. If structure is only visual (bold text that looks like a heading), it is lost.
howToFix: Editors: use the Rich Text Editor's heading and list buttons instead of making text bold or large, and use real tables only for tabular data. Developers: use semantic HTML (h1–h6, ul/ol, table with th, label for inputs, fieldset/legend for groups) in templates and blocks.
caveats: Don't pick a heading level for its size; pick it for its place in the outline and style it with CSS. Layout tables and empty paragraphs used for spacing create false structure.
howToTest: Use a heading/landmark browser extension or a screen reader's headings list: does the outline reflect the page? Check that lists are real lists, data tables have header cells, and every form field has a label you can click.

title: Meaningful Sequence
why: Screen readers and keyboard users follow the code order, not the visual layout. If the order in the code differs from the reading order, content can become confusing.
howToFix: Make the HTML source order match the logical reading order. Use CSS grid/flex for visual placement without reordering meaning, and avoid CSS order or absolute positioning to rearrange content.
caveats: CSS order and grid placement don't change the reading or tab order. Two-column layouts can be read column-by-column; that's fine as long as each column makes sense in sequence.
howToTest: Read the page with CSS turned off (or with a screen reader). Does the content still make sense in the order it appears?

title: Sensory Characteristics
why: Instructions that rely only on shape, colour, size, position or sound ("click the green button on the right") can't be followed by blind users or people who see the page differently.
howToFix: Write instructions that name the thing as well: "Select Send (the green button)" instead of "click the green button". Avoid "see the box to the left" without naming the box.
caveats: Position words are fine when combined with a name. Layouts change on mobile, so "on the right" may be wrong anyway.
howToTest: Read every instruction on the site. Could someone follow it without seeing colour, shape or position?

title: Orientation
why: Some people use a tablet or phone mounted in one orientation, for example on a wheelchair. If the site only works in portrait or landscape, they're locked out.
howToFix: Don't lock the page to one orientation with CSS or JavaScript; make layouts responsive so they work in both.
caveats: Only content where a specific orientation is essential (a piano app, a bank cheque) is exempt.
howToTest: Open the site on a phone or in a device emulator and rotate it. Everything should work and remain readable in both orientations.

title: Identify Input Purpose
why: When form fields declare what they collect (name, email, phone), browsers and assistive tools can fill them in automatically and show familiar icons, which helps people with motor and cognitive disabilities.
howToFix: Add the correct autocomplete attribute to fields that ask for information about the user, e.g. autocomplete="name", "email", "tel", "organization", "street-address", "postal-code".
caveats: Only fields about the user themselves need it, not fields like "recipient's email". Don't set autocomplete="off" on these fields. Message and comment fields have no token.
howToTest: Inspect each form: do name, email, phone, address and similar fields have a matching autocomplete value? Try browser autofill.

title: Identify Purpose
why: When icons, regions and controls declare their purpose in code, tools can adapt them, for example replacing icons with familiar symbols for people with cognitive disabilities.
howToFix: Use landmarks (header, nav, main, footer) and well-named controls consistently, and mark up the purpose of common icons where supporting techniques exist.
caveats: AAA, with limited tool support today. Landmarks and good naming give most of the benefit.
howToTest: Check that landmark regions are used and named, and that common controls and icons have consistent, meaningful names.

title: Use of Color
why: People who are colour blind, and people using high contrast modes, can't tell things apart by colour alone — such as links in body text, required fields marked red, or chart lines.
howToFix: Add a second cue beside colour: underline links in running text, add text or an icon to error states ("Required"), and use patterns, labels or shapes in charts.
caveats: Links that are only a different colour from surrounding text fail unless the contrast between link and text is at least 3:1 and focus/hover adds another cue; underlining is simpler. Editors' coloured text in the Rich Text Editor is affected too.
howToTest: View the page in greyscale (browser DevTools rendering emulation). Can you still find links, errors, required fields and chart series?

title: Audio Control
why: Sound that starts automatically interferes with screen readers, which speak through the same speakers, and can be distressing.
howToFix: Don't autoplay audio. If a video must autoplay, keep it muted, and always provide a visible pause/stop or mute control at the start of the page.
caveats: Background videos with sound are the usual offender. A control that's hard to reach by keyboard doesn't help.
howToTest: Load each page with sound on. If anything plays automatically for more than 3 seconds, check you can stop it with the keyboard right away.

title: Contrast (Minimum)
why: Low contrast text is hard or impossible to read for people with low vision, older users, and anyone in bright sunlight.
howToFix: Make normal text at least 4.5:1 against its background, and large text (24px, or 18.7px bold) at least 3:1. Developers fix this in the design tokens/CSS; check text on images and gradients too.
caveats: Light grey placeholder text, text over photos and white text on brand colours are common failures. Disabled controls and logos are exempt. Automated tools can't measure text over images reliably.
howToTest: Use a contrast checker on body text, links, buttons, placeholders and text over images, in every colour theme the site uses.

title: Resize Text
why: People with low vision zoom text up to 200%. If the layout breaks or text is cut off, content becomes unreadable.
howToFix: Use relative units (rem/em) for font sizes, avoid fixed heights on text containers, and don't disable zoom in the viewport meta tag.
caveats: maximum-scale=1 or user-scalable=no in the viewport tag blocks zoom on mobile. Text inside images doesn't scale.
howToTest: Zoom the browser to 200% and check every page type: no text cut off, overlapping or hidden, and all functions still usable.

title: Images of Text
why: Text in images can't be resized, re-coloured or read by screen readers properly, and it becomes blurry when zoomed.
howToFix: Use real text styled with CSS instead of images of text. Editors: don't upload banners or posters with important text baked in; put the text in the page and use the image as decoration.
caveats: Logos are exempt. If an image of text is unavoidable, its alt text must contain the same text.
howToTest: Look for images that contain words (banners, buttons, quotes, infographics) and check whether the text could have been real text.

title: Contrast (Enhanced)
why: Higher contrast helps people with more severe low vision read text without assistive technology.
howToFix: Make normal text at least 7:1 against its background, and large text at least 4.5:1.
caveats: AAA. It can conflict with brand colours; consider it for body text first.
howToTest: Measure contrast of all text with a contrast checker against the 7:1 / 4.5:1 thresholds.

title: Low or No Background Audio
why: Background music or noise makes speech hard to understand for people who are hard of hearing.
howToFix: In audio recordings with speech, keep background sounds at least 20 dB quieter than the speech, or offer a way to turn them off.
caveats: AAA. Applies to prerecorded audio-only content.
howToTest: Listen to recordings: is the speech clearly louder than any background music or noise?

title: Visual Presentation
why: People with low vision or reading disabilities read more easily when they can control colours and line width, and when text isn't justified or cramped.
howToFix: Keep text columns under about 80 characters, avoid justified text, use line spacing of at least 1.5, and let users change colours (e.g. respect browser and OS settings).
caveats: AAA. A preferences panel can help here, but the site's default layout should already be readable.
howToTest: Check body text for line length, justification and line spacing, and that resizing text to 200% doesn't require horizontal scrolling.

title: Images of Text (No Exception)
why: Same as 1.4.5, without the exceptions: text should always be real text.
howToFix: Replace all images of text with styled text, except logos.
caveats: AAA. Logos and text where a particular presentation is essential are still exempt.
howToTest: Find every image containing text and check it's a logo or essential.

title: Reflow
why: People who zoom to 400% need content to reflow into one column, so they don't have to scroll in two directions to read each line.
howToFix: Build responsive layouts that work at 320 CSS pixels wide without horizontal scrolling. Let tables and wide content scroll inside their own container.
caveats: Data tables, maps and diagrams may scroll horizontally on their own. Fixed headers and cookie banners that take up half the screen at 400% are a common failure.
howToTest: Set the browser window to 1280px wide and zoom to 400%. Read the pages: you should only need to scroll vertically, and nothing should be cut off.

title: Non-text Contrast
why: People with low vision need to see the edges of buttons and form fields, focus indicators, and the parts of icons and charts that carry meaning.
howToFix: Give input borders, icons, focus outlines and chart elements at least 3:1 contrast against what's next to them.
caveats: Light grey input borders and subtle focus rings are common failures. Inactive (disabled) controls are exempt.
howToTest: Measure the contrast of form field borders, buttons without text, icons, focus indicators and chart lines against adjacent colours.

title: Text Spacing
why: People with dyslexia or low vision often increase letter, word and line spacing with a browser extension. If the layout clips or overlaps text, they can't read it.
howToFix: Avoid fixed heights and widths on text containers and let them grow. Test with increased spacing: line height 1.5, paragraph spacing 2× font size, letter spacing 0.12em, word spacing 0.16em.
caveats: Buttons and cards with fixed heights are where text usually gets cut off. You don't have to provide the spacing yourself, only make sure the layout survives it.
howToTest: Apply a text spacing bookmarklet or extension with the values above and check that no text is cut off or overlaps.

title: Content on Hover or Focus
why: Tooltips and menus that appear on hover or focus can cover content for people who zoom, and disappear before slow users can read them.
howToFix: Make popups that appear on hover/focus dismissible with Escape, keep them visible while the pointer is over them, and don't hide them until the user moves away or dismisses them.
caveats: Native title tooltips are controlled by the browser and are exempt, but they're inaccessible to keyboard users anyway; don't put important information in them.
howToTest: Hover and focus elements that show extra content. Can you move the mouse onto the popup without it vanishing? Does Escape close it without moving focus?

title: Keyboard
why: Many people can't use a mouse — blind users, people with tremors or paralysis, and power users. Everything must work with the keyboard alone.
howToFix: Use native links and buttons for anything clickable, never a div or span with a click handler. Custom widgets (menus, sliders, carousels, accordions) need keyboard handling following the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices.
caveats: Hover-only menus, drag-only interactions and clickable cards built from divs are typical failures. Embedded third-party widgets (maps, chat, booking) count too.
howToTest: Put the mouse away. Use Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, Escape and arrow keys to use every menu, form, slider, accordion, video player and the cookie banner.

title: No Keyboard Trap
why: If keyboard focus gets stuck inside an element, a keyboard user can't reach the rest of the page and may have to reload or give up.
howToFix: Make sure focus can always leave a component with Tab, Shift+Tab or Escape. Modal dialogs may hold focus while open but must close with Escape and return focus.
caveats: Embedded iframes (maps, video players, chat widgets) are frequent traps.
howToTest: Tab through the whole page, into and out of every widget and iframe. You must always be able to move on.

title: Keyboard (No Exception)
why: Same as 2.1.1 without exceptions: absolutely everything works by keyboard.
howToFix: Provide keyboard access to all functionality, including things like freehand drawing alternatives.
caveats: AAA.
howToTest: Do every task on the site using only the keyboard.

title: Character Key Shortcuts
why: Single-key shortcuts (like pressing "s" to search) are triggered by accident by speech recognition users and people with tremors.
howToFix: If the site has single-character keyboard shortcuts, let users turn them off or remap them, or only activate them when the relevant component has focus.
caveats: Most websites have no such shortcuts; check third-party widgets.
howToTest: Press single letter and number keys on each page (with focus on the page, not a field). Nothing should happen unexpectedly.

title: Timing Adjustable
why: People who read or type slowly, or use assistive technology, need more time. Time limits can make them lose their work.
howToFix: Avoid time limits. If a session or form times out, warn the user before it happens and let them extend it with a simple action, at least 10 times.
caveats: Login session timeouts, booking holds and auto-advancing content are the usual cases. Real-time events (auctions) are exempt.
howToTest: Look for any timeout. Wait for it: are you warned at least 20 seconds before and offered a way to extend?

title: Pause, Stop, Hide
why: Moving, blinking or auto-updating content distracts people with attention disorders and makes reading impossible for some. It also interferes with screen readers.
howToFix: Give carousels, animations, tickers and background videos that move for more than 5 seconds a visible pause/stop button. Better still, don't autoplay them.
caveats: Respecting prefers-reduced-motion helps but isn't enough on its own; a visible control is required. Animated GIFs uploaded by editors count too.
howToTest: Find all moving content: carousels, videos, animations, GIFs. Each must be pausable with the keyboard, or stop by itself within 5 seconds.

title: No Timing
why: Removing time limits altogether helps everyone who needs more time.
howToFix: Don't use time limits except for real-time events and media.
caveats: AAA.
howToTest: Check that no task on the site has a time limit.

title: Interruptions
why: Interruptions such as pop-ups and auto-updates break concentration, especially for people with cognitive disabilities.
howToFix: Let users postpone or turn off non-emergency interruptions such as newsletter pop-ups, chat prompts and live updates.
caveats: AAA.
howToTest: Use the site for a few minutes. Can you suppress any pop-ups or interruptions that appear?

title: Re-authenticating
why: If a session expires, users should be able to log in again and continue without losing what they entered.
howToFix: Save form data when the session expires and restore it after re-authentication.
caveats: AAA.
howToTest: Let a logged-in session expire mid-form, log in again and check your data is still there.

title: Timeouts
why: People who need breaks should know in advance if inactivity will cause data loss.
howToFix: Warn users how long they can be inactive before data is lost, or keep data for at least 20 hours.
caveats: AAA.
howToTest: Check multi-step forms and logged-in areas for a warning about inactivity timeouts.

title: Three Flashes or Below Threshold
why: Content that flashes more than three times a second can trigger seizures in people with photosensitive epilepsy.
howToFix: Don't use content that flashes more than three times per second. Editors: check videos and GIFs before publishing.
caveats: This is a safety issue, not just usability. Video intros and animated ads are typical sources.
howToTest: Watch all videos, animations and GIFs. Nothing should flash more than three times in one second. Tools like PEAT can analyse video.

title: Three Flashes
why: Stricter version of 2.3.1 with no size threshold.
howToFix: Avoid any content that flashes more than three times per second.
caveats: AAA.
howToTest: Check that nothing flashes more than three times per second.

title: Animation from Interactions
why: Motion triggered by scrolling or clicking (parallax, zooming transitions) can cause nausea and dizziness for people with vestibular disorders.
howToFix: Let users turn off non-essential motion; at minimum respect the prefers-reduced-motion setting and disable parallax and animated transitions when it's on.
caveats: AAA. The package's "Follow browser/OS settings → reduced motion" option helps here but the site's own animations should still honour it.
howToTest: Turn on "reduce motion" in the OS and use the site. Parallax, zooming and sliding transitions should stop.

title: Bypass Blocks
why: Keyboard and screen reader users shouldn't have to tab through the whole header and menu on every page to reach the content.
howToFix: Add a "Skip to main content" link as the first focusable element, visible when focused, and use landmark elements (header, nav, main, footer).
caveats: The skip link must actually move focus to the main content, and must not be permanently hidden.
howToTest: Load a page and press Tab once. A skip link should appear; pressing Enter should move focus to the main content.

title: Page Titled
why: The page title is the first thing a screen reader announces and what appears in tabs, bookmarks and search results. It tells users where they are.
howToFix: Make each page's <title> unique and descriptive, e.g. "Contact us – Company name". Developers build it from the page's name or SEO title in the template; editors make sure page names and SEO titles are meaningful.
caveats: Identical titles on every page, or titles like "Home" on subpages, fail. Put the page-specific part first.
howToTest: Look at the browser tab for each page type. Is the title unique and does it describe the page?

title: Focus Order
why: Keyboard users need focus to move in an order that follows the meaning of the page. Jumping around is disorienting.
howToFix: Keep the DOM order the same as the visual order. Don't use positive tabindex values. When opening dialogs or menus, move focus into them, and return it when they close.
caveats: CSS order and grid placement don't change tab order. Off-screen menus that are still focusable create invisible stops.
howToTest: Tab through each page type and watch where focus goes. It should follow the visual reading order with no jumps or invisible stops.

title: Link Purpose (In Context)
why: Screen reader users often list all links on a page. "Read more", "Click here" repeated ten times tells them nothing.
howToFix: Editors: write link text that says where the link goes ("Read more about our pricing" or just "Pricing"). Developers: for repeated card links, include the card's title in the accessible name, e.g. with visually hidden text.
caveats: aria-label overrides the visible text; keep the visible words at the start of it (see 2.5.3). Links to files should say the file type, e.g. "Annual report (PDF, 2 MB)".
howToTest: List all links on a page (screen reader links list or a bookmarklet). Does each link make sense on its own or with its surrounding sentence?

title: Multiple Ways
why: People find content in different ways: some navigate menus, others search or use a sitemap.
howToFix: Offer at least two ways to find pages, such as main navigation plus site search, a sitemap or an A–Z index.
caveats: Pages that are steps in a process (checkout) are exempt.
howToTest: Check that the site has at least two of: navigation menu, search, sitemap, related links, table of contents.

title: Headings and Labels
why: Clear headings and labels let everyone scan a page and understand form fields, and they're how screen reader users navigate.
howToFix: Editors: write headings that describe the section below. Developers and editors: give form fields labels that say exactly what to enter.
caveats: This criterion is about the wording being descriptive, not about whether headings exist (that's 1.3.1).
howToTest: Read only the headings of a page: do they describe the content? Read only the form labels: is it clear what to enter?

title: Focus Visible
why: Keyboard users need to see where they are on the page. Without a visible focus indicator they're navigating blind.
howToFix: Never remove the focus outline without replacing it. Use :focus-visible to style a clear outline (e.g. 2–3px solid, with good contrast) on links, buttons and form fields.
caveats: outline: none in a CSS reset is the classic failure. Custom components and third-party widgets often lose focus styles.
howToTest: Tab through the page. At every stop, can you clearly see which element has focus?

title: Location
why: Knowing where you are in a site helps people with cognitive disabilities and screen reader users.
howToFix: Show breadcrumbs or highlight the current page in the navigation (with aria-current="page").
caveats: AAA.
howToTest: On deep pages, check that breadcrumbs or a highlighted menu item show the current location.

title: Link Purpose (Link Only)
why: Stricter version of 2.4.4: each link's text alone should say where it goes.
howToFix: Write link text that makes sense out of context, without relying on the surrounding sentence.
caveats: AAA.
howToTest: Read the list of links without context. Each should be understandable.

title: Section Headings
why: Headings that divide long content help everyone scan and help screen reader users jump between sections.
howToFix: Editors: break long texts into sections with headings using the Rich Text Editor's heading styles.
caveats: AAA.
howToTest: Check long pages for headings that divide the content into sections.

title: Focus Not Obscured (Minimum)
why: If a sticky header, cookie banner or chat button covers the element that has focus, keyboard users can't see where they are.
howToFix: Make sure focused elements are never completely hidden by sticky headers, footers or banners. Use scroll-padding-top equal to the sticky header's height, and keep cookie banners from covering focused content.
caveats: New in WCAG 2.2. Cookie banners and sticky headers are the usual causes, especially when zoomed in.
howToTest: Tab through long pages, including with 200% zoom. The focused element must never be completely hidden behind anything.

title: Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced)
why: Stricter version of 2.4.11: the focused element should not be covered at all.
howToFix: Ensure no part of the focused element is hidden by author-created content.
caveats: AAA, new in 2.2.
howToTest: Tab through the page; no part of the focused element should be covered.

title: Focus Appearance
why: A strong focus indicator helps people with low vision find focus quickly.
howToFix: Make the focus indicator at least as large as a 2px outline around the element, with at least 3:1 contrast between focused and unfocused states.
caveats: AAA, new in 2.2.
howToTest: Measure the focus indicator's thickness and contrast on links, buttons and fields.

title: Pointer Gestures
why: People with motor disabilities may not be able to do multi-finger or path-based gestures like pinching or swiping.
howToFix: Provide single-pointer alternatives (buttons) for anything that uses swipe, pinch or multi-finger gestures, such as previous/next buttons on carousels and zoom buttons on maps.
caveats: Browser and OS gestures (like pinch-to-zoom the page) are not your responsibility.
howToTest: On a touch device, check every swipe/pinch interaction also has a button-based alternative.

title: Pointer Cancellation
why: People with tremors often touch the wrong target. Actions that trigger on press-down give them no chance to slide away and cancel.
howToFix: Trigger actions on click/up events (the default for links and buttons), not on mousedown/touchstart.
caveats: Native buttons already behave correctly; custom handlers on pointerdown are the risk.
howToTest: Press on a button, keep holding, move the pointer away and release. The action should not happen.

title: Label in Name
why: Speech recognition users say what they see ("click Send"). If the control's accessible name differs from its visible label, the command doesn't work.
howToFix: Make the accessible name contain the visible label text, ideally at the start. If you use aria-label, include the visible words in it.
caveats: A button showing "Search" with aria-label="Find articles" fails. Icon-only buttons have no visible label, so this doesn't apply to them.
howToTest: Compare visible labels with accessible names (in DevTools' accessibility pane). The visible text should appear in the name.

title: Motion Actuation
why: Functions triggered by shaking or tilting a device can't be used by people with the device mounted, and can be triggered accidentally by tremors.
howToFix: Provide a normal control for anything triggered by device motion, and let users turn motion triggers off.
caveats: Rare on websites.
howToTest: Check whether anything on the site responds to shaking or tilting; if so, find the alternative control.

title: Target Size (Enhanced)
why: Large targets help people with tremors, limited dexterity or large fingers — for example someone with Parkinson's.
howToFix: Make clickable targets at least 44×44 CSS pixels. The package's "Bigger buttons and more spacing" visitor option can enlarge targets for those who need it, but the default design should aim for this.
caveats: AAA. Links inside a sentence are exempt.
howToTest: Measure buttons, icons and menu items. Each should be at least 44×44 pixels.

title: Concurrent Input Mechanisms
why: People switch between mouse, keyboard, touch and other input. A site shouldn't restrict which input is used.
howToFix: Don't disable mouse input on touch devices or vice versa.
caveats: AAA.
howToTest: On a touch laptop, use the site with touch, mouse and keyboard interchangeably.

title: Dragging Movements
why: Dragging requires holding a button while moving precisely, which many people with motor disabilities can't do.
howToFix: Give every drag interaction (sliders, sortable lists, maps, upload drop zones) a single-pointer alternative, such as buttons, clicks or a text field.
caveats: New in WCAG 2.2. A file drop zone needs a normal "Choose file" button too.
howToTest: Find every drag-and-drop interaction. Can you do the same thing with simple clicks or taps?

title: Target Size (Minimum)
why: Small targets placed close together are hard to hit for people with tremors or limited dexterity, such as people with Parkinson's, and cause wrong clicks.
howToFix: Make targets at least 24×24 CSS pixels, or space them so that a 24px circle centred on each doesn't overlap another target. Pay special attention to icon buttons, close buttons, pagination and social icons.
caveats: New in WCAG 2.2. Links in running text and controls whose size the browser sets are exempt. 24px is the minimum; 44px (2.5.5) is much better for motor impairments.
howToTest: Measure small controls in DevTools. Each must be 24×24px or have enough space around it.

title: Language of Page
why: Screen readers choose pronunciation from the page's language. With the wrong language, Swedish text read with English rules is unintelligible.
howToFix: Set the lang attribute on the <html> element to the page's culture, e.g. lang="sv" or lang="en". In Umbraco templates, output the current culture of the page.
caveats: On multilingual sites each culture variant must set its own language, not a hard-coded value.
howToTest: View the page source and check that <html lang="…"> matches the page's language.

title: Language of Parts
why: When a page mixes languages, screen readers need to switch pronunciation for the foreign passages.
howToFix: Editors: mark passages in another language. Developers: give editors a way to do this in the Rich Text Editor (a lang attribute on a span or block), and set lang on components that show content in another culture.
caveats: Single loanwords and proper names don't need marking. Whole quotes or paragraphs in another language do.
howToTest: Find passages in a different language from the page and check they're wrapped in an element with the right lang attribute.

title: Unusual Words
why: Jargon, idioms and unusual words can block understanding for people with cognitive disabilities and non-native readers.
howToFix: Explain unusual words and jargon, for example in the text, in a glossary or with definitions.
caveats: AAA.
howToTest: Read the content for jargon or unusual terms and check they're explained.

title: Abbreviations
why: Abbreviations can be unclear to many readers.
howToFix: Write out abbreviations the first time they appear, or link to an explanation.
caveats: AAA.
howToTest: Check that abbreviations are expanded or explained.

title: Reading Level
why: Complex text excludes people with reading or cognitive disabilities.
howToFix: When text needs more than lower-secondary reading ability, add a simpler summary or an easy-to-read version.
caveats: AAA. Many Swedish public sites publish "lättläst" versions.
howToTest: Check the reading level of key pages, and whether simpler versions or summaries exist.

title: Pronunciation
why: Some words are ambiguous without knowing their pronunciation.
howToFix: Provide pronunciation where meaning depends on it.
caveats: AAA. Rarely relevant.
howToTest: Look for words whose meaning depends on pronunciation and check it's provided.

title: On Focus
why: If moving focus to something triggers a big change (a new page, a popup), keyboard and screen reader users lose their place.
howToFix: Don't open windows, submit forms or navigate when an element merely receives focus. Only act when the user activates it.
caveats: Focus-triggered popups and auto-opening menus are typical.
howToTest: Tab through all controls. Nothing should happen just because something received focus.

title: On Input
why: Changing a setting shouldn't unexpectedly reload the page or move users elsewhere; that confuses screen reader and keyboard users.
howToFix: Don't submit forms or navigate when a select, radio or checkbox changes. Use a submit button, or clearly say beforehand what will happen.
caveats: Language and filter dropdowns that navigate on change are common failures.
howToTest: Change every dropdown, radio button and checkbox. The page shouldn't navigate or reload unless you were told it would.

title: Consistent Navigation
why: Consistent navigation helps people with cognitive disabilities and screen reader users learn where things are.
howToFix: Keep menus and repeated navigation in the same place and order on every page.
caveats: Items can be added or hidden, but the relative order must stay the same.
howToTest: Compare navigation across several page types: same position, same order.

title: Consistent Identification
why: If the same function has different names on different pages, users think they're different things.
howToFix: Use the same labels and icons for the same function across the site (e.g. always "Search", not "Find" on some pages).
caveats: This includes alt text on repeated icons.
howToTest: Compare repeated components (search, share, download, contact) across pages; their names should match.

title: Change on Request
why: Changes should only happen when the user asks for them.
howToFix: Avoid automatic redirects, auto-opening new windows and auto-refresh; let users trigger changes.
caveats: AAA.
howToTest: Check for automatic redirects, refreshes or new windows.

title: Consistent Help
why: People who need help should find it in the same place on every page, without hunting for it.
howToFix: If the site offers help (contact details, a contact form, chat, FAQ link), put it in the same relative place on every page, typically the header or footer.
caveats: New in WCAG 2.2. It doesn't require help to exist, only consistency if it does.
howToTest: Compare the location of contact/help links across page types; it should be consistent.

title: Error Identification
why: If a form error is only shown by a red border, screen reader and colour-blind users don't know what went wrong.
howToFix: Describe errors in text next to the field ("Enter an email address in the format name@example.com") and connect them with aria-describedby. Move focus to an error summary or the first invalid field.
caveats: Errors must be announced to screen readers, not just shown. Colour alone fails 1.4.1 as well.
howToTest: Submit each form with empty and invalid values. Is each error described in text and announced by a screen reader?

title: Labels or Instructions
why: Users need to know what to enter before they fill a field, including format and which fields are required.
howToFix: Give every field a visible label, mark required fields in text (not only with colour or an asterisk without explanation), and state formats (e.g. "Date (YYYY-MM-DD)").
caveats: Placeholder text is not a label: it disappears when typing and usually has low contrast.
howToTest: Look at each form before filling it in. Is it clear what each field wants and which are required?

title: Error Suggestion
why: Telling users how to fix an error helps people with cognitive disabilities complete forms.
howToFix: When an error is detected and you know the fix, say it: "Postcode must be 5 digits" rather than "Invalid input".
caveats: Don't suggest fixes that weaken security (e.g. revealing which part of a login was wrong).
howToTest: Trigger errors in each form and check the messages explain how to fix them.

title: Error Prevention (Legal, Financial, Data)
why: Mistakes in legal, financial or data submissions can have serious consequences, so users need a chance to check.
howToFix: For purchases, legal agreements or submissions that change user data, let users review and correct before submitting, confirm with a checkbox, or undo afterwards.
caveats: Only applies to forms with legal, financial or data-changing consequences.
howToTest: Go through orders, bookings and account changes. Is there a review step, confirmation or way to undo?

title: Help
why: Context-sensitive help reduces errors for people with cognitive disabilities.
howToFix: Add help text or examples next to complex fields.
caveats: AAA.
howToTest: Check complex forms for helpful instructions and examples.

title: Error Prevention (All)
why: Extends 3.3.4 to every form that submits information.
howToFix: Let users review, confirm or undo every form submission.
caveats: AAA.
howToTest: Check all forms for a review, confirmation or undo option.

title: Redundant Entry
why: Re-entering the same information is hard for people with memory or motor disabilities and causes errors.
howToFix: In multi-step processes, don't ask for the same information twice: pre-fill it or offer a choice like "Billing address same as delivery".
caveats: New in WCAG 2.2. Re-entering a password for security is allowed.
howToTest: Go through multi-step forms. Is any information asked for again that you already gave?

title: Accessible Authentication (Minimum)
why: Logins that require remembering or transcribing things (puzzles, retyping codes, solving tasks) lock out people with cognitive disabilities.
howToFix: Allow password managers and paste in login fields, support copy-paste of one-time codes, and avoid cognitive tests such as puzzle CAPTCHAs. Offer alternatives such as login links by email or passkeys.
caveats: New in WCAG 2.2. Blocking paste in password fields fails. Object-recognition CAPTCHAs are allowed at AA but not AAA.
howToTest: Log in using a password manager and by pasting the password. Check that any CAPTCHA or verification step has an alternative that doesn't require solving a puzzle.

title: Accessible Authentication (Enhanced)
why: Stricter version of 3.3.8: no cognitive tests at all, including object recognition.
howToFix: Remove all cognitive function tests from login, or provide an alternative without one.
caveats: AAA, new in 2.2.
howToTest: Check authentication steps for any recognition or memory test.

title: Parsing
why: Older assistive technology parsed HTML itself and could break on invalid markup such as duplicate ids or unclosed tags.
howToFix: Produce valid HTML: unique ids, properly nested and closed elements, no duplicate attributes.
caveats: Obsolete and removed in WCAG 2.2, because browsers now repair markup consistently. It still counts when measuring against 2.0 or 2.1.
howToTest: Run the page through the W3C validator and check for duplicate ids and nesting errors.

title: Name, Role, Value
why: Screen readers and voice control need to know what every control is (button, checkbox, tab), what it's called, and its state (checked, expanded).
howToFix: Use native HTML elements wherever possible. For custom widgets, add the correct ARIA role, an accessible name and states such as aria-expanded, aria-pressed or aria-selected, and keep them updated.
caveats: No ARIA is better than wrong ARIA. Icon buttons without names and accordions without aria-expanded are typical failures. Automated tools only catch part of this.
howToTest: Use a screen reader on menus, accordions, tabs, modals and custom form controls. Each should announce its role, name and current state, and the state should change when you use it.

title: Status Messages
why: Messages that appear without moving focus ("Added to cart", "3 results", "Saved") are missed by screen reader users unless they're announced.
howToFix: Put status messages in a live region (role="status" or aria-live="polite"; role="alert" for errors) that exists in the page before the message is inserted.
caveats: A live region added at the same moment as its text is often not announced. Don't overuse alerts.
howToTest: With a screen reader, trigger search results, form confirmations and cart updates. The message should be read out without you moving focus.
